title: Clozapine Intoxication Mimicking Acute Stroke
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
case_prompt:
A 66-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia was brought to the emergency department by his wife for altered mental status. Two hours before arrival, he had consumed two glasses of wine and taken a nap; he was asymptomatic before the nap. On awakening, he exhibited dysarthria and extremity discoordination.

Home medications included bupropion, dutasteride, lisinopril, and tolterodine. 

Vital signs were: blood pressure 115/78 mm Hg, heart rate 83 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.8 °C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air.

On examination, he had waxing and waning alertness but could intermittently follow commands. Pupils were reactive but sluggish, with horizontal and vertical nystagmus. Facial symmetry was intact, the tongue was midline, and speech was dysarthric. Motor strength could not be formally assessed; he moved all extremities symmetrically. He had bilateral dysmetria on finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing and truncal ataxia when seated.

During approximately 1.5 hours in the ED, his ataxia and mental status progressively worsened. A stroke alert was activated, and a head CT angiogram was negative for hemorrhage or other abnormalities. Laboratory studies, including a complete blood count, chemistry panel, coagulation studies, and urinalysis, were within normal limits. His blood alcohol concentration was 57 mg/dL. Electrocardiography showed normal sinus rhythm with a QRS duration of 108 ms and a QTc of 497 ms. Naloxone, 0.4 mg IV, produced no improvement.

Neurology evaluation yielded an NIH Stroke Scale score of 11; tissue plasminogen activator was administered for presumed posterior circulation stroke. The patient was intubated for airway protection and admitted to the intensive care unit.

In the ICU, he developed status epilepticus with three 5-minute episodes of generalized tonic–clonic seizures. He received benzodiazepines, phenytoin, and a propofol infusion, after which seizure activity ceased. Subsequent EEG showed no ongoing seizures.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain did not show evidence of acute stroke.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute ischemic stroke — “Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain did not show evidence of acute stroke.”  
2. Alcohol-withdrawal seizure — “An alcohol-withdrawal seizure was thought to be less likely as the patient did not have a history of heavy alcohol use or alcohol withdrawal, nor did he demonstrate symptoms consistent with alcohol withdrawal.”  
3. Dystonic reaction — “It is also possible that the patient’s abnormal movements were the result of a dystonic reaction, but this would be unusual given the relative low affinity for D2 antagonism of clozapine as compared to typical antipsychotics.”  
4. Clozapine intoxication — “Comprehensive urine drug screen by gas chromatography and mass spectrometry was positive for clozapine and clozapine metabolites… However, the patient had never been prescribed clozapine.”
